messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel is a 34-year-old school counselor who came to treatment nearly a year after a car accident in which he struck a teenage pedestrian outside a medical office complex near his school district. He had been driving home after a long, tense day, distracted and keyed up, when the boy stepped off the curb between parked cars. Daniel still remembers the sweet chemical smell drifting from the clinic’s open doorway, the flash of a white exam-paper gown through the glass, and the sickening thud that followed before he had fully understood what he had done. The boy survived but was seriously injured. Daniel can say the facts in fragments, but whenever he tries to tell the story in order, the words disappear. What comes back instead is not a narrative but a total reliving: the smell, the sight of the body on the pavement, the sound of shouting, all of it arriving as if it is happening now. In the weeks after the accident, everyday strain began to feel dangerous to him. A hard day at school, a parent conflict, even the pressured noise of students moving through the hallway could make him feel as if he were back in the seconds before impact. Because he had come to see himself as someone who failed under pressure, stress no longer registered as ordinary strain; it snagged his attention as evidence, and that made crowded hallways, sharp voices, and rushed moments far more likely to set off reminders of the accident. Medical settings became especially potent. If he had to accompany a student to the nurse’s office, or if he passed the district clinic and caught the disinfectant smell, his body reacted immediately; his chest tightened, his skin went cold, and the scene returned in full sensory detail. In those moments he was flooded not only with the accident itself but with the conviction that it had happened because of the way he acted. The conviction was not separate from the reliving; telling himself that he was the kind of man who could do this made the memory easier to reach and harsher when it came, as if the scene kept returning to prove what he believed about himself. He had come to believe that he could not trust himself to do the right thing under pressure, and each trigger seemed to prove it again. That belief hardened over time into something broader and more devastating. Daniel was certain that his life had been destroyed by what he had done. He no longer saw himself as a careful, dependable person but as someone fundamentally unsafe, the kind of man who could ruin another family in a single careless moment. Because he viewed his own judgment as untrustworthy, he worked constantly to keep his mind occupied: podcasts in the car, grading or email late into the evening, television on in the background, anything to prevent a quiet moment in which the accident might come back. He also went out of his way to avoid police cars, officers at school events, or even news stories about investigations, because contact with police immediately pulled him toward the thought that he should have been punished more harshly. Needing this much distraction and detouring became its own kind of proof to him that he was not steady anymore; every workaround quietly confirmed his fear that he could not cope like other people and that something fundamental in him had been damaged. He tried not to think about the event at all, yet the effort itself seemed to keep it close, and afterward he felt even more ashamed that he was still living this way. The avoidance had also spread the accident across his daily map: the clinic he skirted, the officers he watched for, the stories he skipped all became reminders in their own right, so that more and more of ordinary life carried the outline of what had happened. At work this pattern has become woven into his days. As a counselor he is often the adult students come to when they are distressed, but heightened stress in his office now makes him scan himself and the room as if some fresh catastrophe is about to happen. That same keyed-up sense of imminent disaster kept the accident close by in his mind; once he was on alert, the memory was much harder to hold off and could break through with very little warning. When the sense of danger rose that quickly, stepping back, keeping busy, and finding a reason to leave felt like the only practical way to get through the moment without being overwhelmed. If a student has a panic attack and the nurse is called, Daniel finds reasons to step into the hall rather than stay near the cot, the latex gloves, the alcohol wipes. He tells himself he is giving staff space, though he knows he is escaping the smell and the medical routine that can make the accident burst back with such force. Because he almost never stayed long enough to learn that these moments could pass safely, his body kept treating them as genuinely dangerous, and the threat in medical situations remained as sharp as ever. The more he avoids these situations, the less confidence he has in his ability to handle them, and that loss of confidence sharpens his sense that he is damaged beyond repair. Nights are often the worst. Daniel has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to stay alert, as if relaxing would leave him unguarded against the memory. In bed, any rise in tension can become its own trigger; once he notices his body is keyed up, he braces for the accident to return, and it often does. When the memory surges, it arrives with such immediacy that he feels he is again at the wheel, smelling antiseptic and hearing the impact, and the terror and guilt hit his body at full strength. Afterward he lies awake monitoring every sound in the house, ashamed and angry with himself for not being able to control his own mind. Each time that happened, the thought that followed was painfully familiar: if the accident could still take over his mind like this, then maybe he really was as unsafe and permanently altered as he feared. To avoid that spiral he scrolls on his phone, watches videos, or mentally jumps to tomorrow’s tasks, but the exhaustion leaves him more stressed the next day, more reactive, and more vulnerable to the same intrusions. By the time he sought help, Daniel’s world had narrowed around these efforts to prevent remembering. His wife had begun telling him that even when he was home, he seemed elsewhere, always busy, unreachable, tense. What finally brought him in was a routine physical for himself: sitting in an exam room on crinkling paper, breathing in the smell of disinfectant, he felt the accident engulf him so completely that he had to leave before the doctor came in. He was shaken not only by the reliving but by what it seemed to confirm—that he could not trust himself, that one event had ruined his life, and that he might never again be the steady person his students and family believed him to be. What he hopes for now, cautiously, is not to forget, but to find a way for the memory to become past instead of something he has to survive over and over. And once the memory had broken through in the night, the next day was full of fresh points of contact with it; ordinary tension, a slammed door, even the smell of cleaning products seemed more charged, as though the reliving had taught his attention to keep finding pieces of the accident everywhere.
